text.p: Turkish central bank funded banks on Monday afternoon after draining surplus cash earlier in the day to control money rates, bankers said.

They said the bank also sold dollars for lira with Tuesday value in late trade to restraint demand for the U.S. currency amid political concerns ahead of parliamentary votes on corruption probes against Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller.

The central bank lent banks 14.2 trillion lira at 72 percent overnight and seven trillion lira via tomorrow/next deals at 67 percent. In the morning, it withdrew 25.4 trillion lira of a 44.5 trillion surplus by selling seven-day reverse repos at 94.79 percent average yield in an open market auction.

Overnight money rates which opened at 70 percent firmed gradually after the reverse repo sale which buoyed cash demand. The average overnight money rate was 71.48 percent, unchanged from Friday when the central bank had funded 13.9 trillion lira overnight and seven trillion lira via t/n.
Turkish lira closed firmer at 120,810 to the dollar (with Tuesday value) on central bank intervention, compared to a low of 120,900 at the opening, but was weaker than Friday's 119,840 close.

Bankers said afternoon demand pushed up the U.S. currency to 120,880, prompting central bank's dollar sales for lira towards the close. The lira had earlier firmed to 120,800 at midday on rising cash demand after the reverse repo auction.
"There was some dollar demand in the afternoon. So the central bank stepped in to restrain the dollar's rise," said one private bank dealer.

Bond yields which jumped by around six points in early trade to brush a high of 95 percent due to selling boosted by political concerns, edged lower in the afternoon to 93-94 percent levels on fresh buying, bankers said.

The average yield on the most heavily traded November 19 paper rose to 93.67 percent from Friday's 89.79. The second most active November 26 yielded 93.37 percent, versus Friday's 89.33 percent average.
The average overnight repo rate dropped to 68.96 percent from 71.62 percent on Friday, due to easier money rates and excess liquidity before the reverse repo auction.

Turkish parliament will vote on two corruption allegations against Ciller on Tuesday and another one on Wednesday. All probes were previously rejected by parliamentary commissions, but a vote in the general assembly will be final.
Markets are also unnerved by two censure motions filed by leftist parties against the Islamist-led goverment, scheduled to be taken up in parliament on February 25.
